```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
import {csv, json, pct, num, count, unit, longDate, isoDate, plural, h, reasonBars} from "./lib.js"
head = json("data/ontime/headline.json")
fc = json("data/ontime/field-check.json")
import {d3} from "./vendor/plot-0.6.11/plot.js"
quality = csv(d3, "data/quality/daily.csv")
ontime = csv(d3, "data/ontime/daily.csv")
lastQ = quality.filter(d => String(d.service_expected).toLowerCase() !== "false").at(-1) ?? null
lastO = ontime.filter(d => String(d.service_expected).toLowerCase() !== "false").at(-1) ?? null
day = lastO && isoDate(lastO.service_date) ? json(`data/ontime/days/${isoDate(lastO.service_date)}.json`) : null
hc = head?.current ?? null
// A figure in a sentence, or a plain word when it is not there.
say = (value, format) => value == null || Number.isNaN(value) ? "not yet known" : format(value)
when = lastQ ? longDate(lastQ.service_date) : "the latest day"
```

These figures are careful estimates, not official numbers. This page says
where they come from, what they can tell you, and where they fall short, so
you can judge them for yourself. Each figure on this page is read from the
same published files as the rest of the site.

## Where the data comes from

Every Island Transit bus sends its location to a live feed, and the feed
also says which trip the bus is on and when it expects to reach each stop.
Trip planning apps read this feed. Island Transit does not keep it, and each
update replaces the one before. Our collector, a small program on a free
database service, checks the feed every 20 seconds, day and night, and saves
what it says. It has done so since November 19, 2026. The schedule comes from the same
company that runs the feed, Passio, and is saved twice a day.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p>On ${when}, the collector got a good answer to ${say(lastQ?.vehicle_uptime, x => pct(x, 1))} of its requests for bus locations, and ${say(lastQ?.trip_coverage, x => pct(x, 1))} of the trips on the schedule showed up in the feed.</p>`
```

## How a departure is timed

The feed never says when a bus left a stop. Our script works it out from
where the bus was just before and just after it passed, about 20 seconds
apart. We only score the stops Island Transit prints in its timetables, its
timepoints, because those are the times the agency promises. A bus counts as
on time if it leaves from 1 minute early to 5 minutes late. A departure we
could not time is never counted as late; it is left out and counted apart.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p>Over the last ${say(hc?.days, count)} days with service, we put a time on ${say(hc?.observed_share, x => pct(x, 1))} of the departures at timepoints. The rest are the main gap in these figures: we can't say whether those buses were on time.</p>`
```

## How sure are we? {#how-sure}

A figure can be off for three different reasons, so the home page gives
three ranges under "How sure are we?".

The first is chance. The days we have are a sample of how the buses run,
and a different handful of days would give a slightly different share. To
see how much, our script makes 2,000 new sets of trips by drawing at random
from the real ones, works out the on-time share of each, and keeps the
middle 95% of those shares.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
iv = hc?.on_time_share_interval95
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
iv?.low != null ? html`<p>Over the last ${say(hc?.days, count)} days with service, the share was ${pct(hc.on_time_share_of_observed, 1)}, and allowing for chance it is very likely between ${pct(iv.low, 1)} and ${pct(iv.high, 1)}.</p>` : html``
```

The second is the departures we could not time. Our share counts only the
departures we timed. If the buses we missed ran differently, for example
because tracking breaks down more often in the evening, the share leans one
way. So our script also works out a weighted share, the way surveys adjust
for people who didn't answer. It sorts every scheduled departure by its
route, the time of day and its place along the trip, and lets each timed
departure stand in for the missed ones like it. The weighted share is shown
only while no timed departure has to stand in for ten or more.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
adj = hc?.adjusted
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
adj?.value != null ? html`<p>${adj.shown ? `Weighted this way, about ${pct(adj.value, 1)} of all scheduled departures left on time${adj.interval95 ? `, very likely between ${pct(adj.interval95.low, 1)} and ${pct(adj.interval95.high, 1)}` : ""}.` : "Some groups of departures have too few timed ones to stand in for the rest, so the weighted share is not shown yet."} It still assumes that the buses we missed ran like the ones we timed on the same route, at the same time of day and at the same place along the trip.</p>` : html``
```

The third is the worst case, which assumes nothing at all about the
departures we missed. If every one had been late, the share of scheduled
departures that left on time would be at its lowest; if every one had been
on time, at its highest. The true share lies somewhere in between, whatever
those buses did.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
hc?.bounds?.low != null ? html`<p>Over the same days, that range runs from ${pct(hc.bounds.low, 1)} to ${pct(hc.bounds.high, 1)} of the ${say(hc.scheduled, count)} scheduled departures.</p>` : html``
```

Our script also records why each missed departure has no time: the feed
went quiet near the stop, the bus left out a part of the route that the
schedule includes, the bus stopped reporting before it got there, the trip
sent nothing at all, or the bus was already past the stop when it first
reported. The Data quality page follows each reason over time.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
hc?.untimed ? html`<p>Why ${count(hc.untimed.departures)} departures weren't timed over the last ${say(hc?.days, count)} days with service:</p>${reasonBars(hc.untimed)}` : html``
```

## What we can't see

Some first and last stops are hard to time. Buses start the day at the
depot between Greenbank and Coupeville and drive to their first stop. During
the day one bus often runs several routes, and drivers sometimes change
partway along a route. The feed's trip name changes at those moments, often
a little early or late. Since November 27, 2026, our script follows each bus
rather than each trip name, which cut the last stops we could not time by
more than half. Buses also wait in bays up to 160 meters (about 520 feet)
from where the schedule puts the first or last stop, so since November 28,
2026, a bus coming within 100 meters (about 330 feet) of such a stop counts as
there. On the six days to November 25, that raised the last stops we could
time from 73% to 90%, about as often as the stops in between.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
day?.continuity == null ? html`` : html`<p>On ${lastO ? longDate(lastO.service_date) : "the latest day"}, ${say(day?.continuity?.trips_with_borrowed_reports, n => plural(n, "trip"))} used locations their bus sent under another trip's name, and ${say(day?.continuity?.vehicles_on_two_or_more_routes, n => plural(n, "bus", "buses"))} ran two or more routes.</p>`
```

GPS sometimes puts a bus somewhere it can't be. When a bus seems to jump
faster than 130 km/h (about 80 mph) to a spot and straight back, our script
leaves that location out. A jump with no jump back stays in and is counted,
because we can't tell which side is wrong.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p>On ${when}, ${say(lastQ?.glitch_reports_removed, n => plural(n, "location"))} ${lastQ?.glitch_reports_removed === 1 ? "was" : "were"} left out this way, and ${say(lastQ?.unresolved_jumps, n => plural(n, "jump"))} stayed in.</p>`
```

The feed has never marked a trip as canceled, so a bus that did not run
looks the same as a bus whose tracking failed. We would count a canceled
trip apart the day the feed starts saying so.

## How we check ourselves

Our script compares every departure time it works out with the feed's own
note of which stop the bus is heading for. We also time buses in person on
route 60 and compare. Before the site is rebuilt each night, other checks
make sure every number on it adds up from the day files, and the site keeps
the previous night's figures if they don't.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p>On ${lastO ? longDate(lastO.service_date) : "the latest day"}, ${say(lastO?.feed_agreement_share, x => pct(x, 1))} of our departure times agreed with the feed within 30 seconds. Timed in person, our times were off by ${say(fc?.overall?.mae_s, x => unit(x, "second", 1))} on average, over ${say(fc?.overall?.n, count)} moments, all on route 60.</p>`
```

### Nothing unchecked reaches the site {#gate}

Each night our programs write their new figures to a holding copy of the
data first. Then a set of automatic rules, our publishing gate, checks that
copy. The rules make sure every total adds up from the day files, that no bus
is in two places at once, that every file we point to is really there with
the same contents, and that every table matches its description. Only when
every rule passes do the figures move to the public copy of the data, the
one this site, the examples and anyone downloading the data read. If a rule
fails, the public copy and this site keep the last figures that passed, and
we get a note naming the rule.

The gate's own report sits beside the data as `checks/gate.json`. It lists
the rules it ran, what they found, and when. The comparisons with other bus
systems and the reports from the official feed validators are added during
the day; they pass the first eight rules at once and the whole gate the next
night.

The large files, such as each day's bus positions and departures, are kept
on GitHub. Each new one gets a name that includes a short fingerprint of its
contents, so a rebuilt file is saved beside the old one instead of over it,
and an old file is removed only after the public copy has stopped pointing
to it.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
build = json("data/build.json")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
build?.gate?.rules ? html`<p>The figures on this site passed all ${count(build.gate.rules)} rules on ${longDate(build.gate.ran_at.slice(0, 10))}.</p>` : html``
```

### Anyone can rebuild a day {#rebuild}

Every figure here comes from the saved feed and the code in our repository,
so anyone can make it again. Once a week, a fresh computer at GitHub picks
three past days at random, rebuilds each one from its raw files with the
current code, and compares every file it makes with the published one. The
same code on the same raw files should give the same bytes, down to the last
digit, on any machine.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
rb = build?.reproduce
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
rb ? html`<p>Last independent rebuild: ${plural(rb.days.length, "day")} (${rb.days.map(d => longDate(d)).join(", ")}) rebuilt from raw on ${longDate(rb.ran_at.slice(0, 10))}, ${rb.all_identical ? "every file identical" : "and some files differed; we are looking into it"}.</p>` : html`<p>The first weekly rebuild has not run yet.</p>`
```

To rebuild a day yourself, install Python, download our repository, and run
one command with any day you like:

```bash
pip install -e .
python scripts/reproduce.py --date 2026-11-20
```

It downloads that day's raw files, checks each one against its published
fingerprint, rebuilds the day, and prints whether every file came out the
same, with the day's main figures side by side.

We also checked the schedule itself. On November 27, 2026, we compared
3,015 times printed in Island Transit's September 27, 2026 guide with the
schedule the feed follows: 96.7% matched exactly and 99.3% within a minute,
and most of the rest look like typing errors in the guide.

## What these figures can't tell you

They can't tell you why a bus was late, how long anyone waited, or how
crowded a bus was. They cover the stops Island Transit prints in its
timetables, not every stop. They start on November 19, 2026, so they can't
say how service compares with earlier years. And they rest on one feed: if
it reports wrong locations in a way our checks don't catch, our figures are
wrong too. The [Methods](methods.qmd) page has the full details.

## How far the comparisons go {#comparisons}

The [Compare](compare.qmd) page sets Island Transit beside two Washington
neighbors, Skagit Transit and Intercity Transit. We time their buses with
our own method, from two-hour samples of their live feeds taken on Tuesdays
and Thursdays around midday, and pool the samples of the last eight weeks.
That is a small slice of their service: it misses early mornings, evenings
and weekends, and each agency picks its own timepoints. Samples taken on a
federal holiday or the day before or after one are left out, because
service and traffic are unusual then. The first samples, on November 27,
2026, the day after Thanksgiving, were left out this way, so the first
pooled figures come from the samples of December 1, 2026.

The Compare page also counts our own buses a little more strictly than the
home page does. The home page counts a bus that reaches the end of its trip
early as on time; the Compare page counts it as early, the way most
agencies do, so that both sides are counted alike. Over November 19 to 25,
2026, that moved our figure from 74.2% to 70.0%. A check before every
update makes sure the two figures differ by exactly the number of those
early arrivals.

## Spotted something off? {#feedback}

If a figure looks wrong, a page doesn't work, or you have a question about
the data, please [tell us on GitHub](https://github.com/dfladagermccullugh-bot/Open-Island-Transit-Data/issues/new/choose).
You pick a short form, say what you saw, and it goes on the project's public
list of issues, where anyone can read the answer. Sending one needs a free
GitHub account. We don't publish an email address, so that every question
and every fix stays in the open next to the code and the data. Questions
about the buses themselves, such as fares, schedules or a lost item, go to
[Island Transit](https://www.islandtransit.org/), since this project is
independent of it.
